summary: For ages 7–9, teach Earth's three named layers (crust, mantle, core) on a single labelled cutaway, then land the two real payloads: the crust is astonishingly THIN relative to the whole planet, and Earth's inside gets HOTTER with depth until it is hot enough to melt rock. Lead with a tap-to-reveal cutaway sphere that drills inward; support it with a driveable depth/temperature descent for a felt sense of thinness and heat, a nested 3D globe for scale extension, and a consolidation activity for naming and order. Guard against misconceptions that the crust is thick, that the whole interior is runny lava, or that the centre is hollow/cool — noting that much of the interior is solid rock and only the outer core is truly liquid.
misconceptions: The crust is thick / a large fraction of the Earth (it is a very thin skin by comparison).
The whole inside of the Earth is liquid lava/molten rock (much of the interior is solid or very stiff rock; the outer core is liquid metal, the inner core solid).
The centre is hollow, or filled with air/water, or that people/creatures could live inside.
'Lava' fills the Earth (magma forms only in specific hot regions; the term 'lava' applies only at the surface).
The layers are cold like ordinary underground soil (the interior is extremely hot, increasing with depth).

activities.title: Drill-down cutaway: name the layers and feel the thin crust
steps: Look at one labelled cutaway sphere of Earth showing crust, mantle and core named from the outside in.

Tap the crust to reveal its fact card (a thin rocky skin we stand on), tap the mantle to reveal 'thick, very hot, slow-flowing rock (mostly solid)', and tap the core to reveal 'the hottest part — a ball of iron whose outer part is liquid metal and whose very centre is solid'.
Lift a flap on the crust asking 'How thick is the crust really?' which zooms OUT and redraws the crust as a hair-thin line around the whole planet, captioned 'as thin as the skin on an apple'.
Say the three layers aloud from the outside in: crust, mantle, core.
activities.insight: Earth has three concentric layers, and the crust we live on is a very thin skin compared with the thick hot mantle and central core.

activities.title: Drill to the centre: hotter with depth
steps: Drive a descending drill from the surface toward the centre, watching a live depth gauge and a temperature gauge.
Notice the crust is crossed almost immediately while the temperature keeps climbing — passing a marked point labelled 'hot enough to melt rock'.
Let each layer name itself (crust, mantle, core) as the drill passes it.
Afterwards, read a to-scale bar showing how little of the whole journey was the crust.
activities.insight: The deeper you go, the hotter it gets — hot enough to melt rock — and the crust occupies only a tiny fraction of the distance to the centre.

activities.title: Nested globe (scale extension)
steps: Rotate a cut-open 3D globe to see the layers as concentric shells drawn to scale.
Pinch-zoom on the outer shell to feel how thin the crust is relative to the whole sphere.
Describe in your own words how much of the globe is crust versus everything beneath.
activities.insight: Earth is a nested sphere of concentric shells, and the crust shell is extremely thin compared with the interior.

activities.title: Consolidate names, order and facts
steps: Sequence the layers from outside in: crust → mantle → core.
Answer 'Which layer is thinnest?' and 'Which is hottest?'
Use a slider to answer 'How hot is it deep down — warm, boiling, or hot enough to melt rock?'
Label a blank cutaway diagram with crust, mantle and core.
activities.insight: The learner can reliably recall the three layer names, their order, which is thinnest, and that the interior is hot enough to melt rock.

checkQuestion: Imagine a slice cut through the whole Earth, from the surface down to the centre. Which layer are we standing on, and how thick is it compared with the layers underneath?
checkAnswer: We stand on the crust, the outermost layer. It's extremely THIN compared with the layers below — like the skin on an apple compared with the whole apple. Beneath it is the thick, very hot mantle, and at the centre the core. The inside of the Earth is hot enough to melt rock.
